newsitem.title: USA: Pathfinder spacecraft nears July 4 rendezvous with Mars.
newsitem.headline: Pathfinder spacecraft nears July 4 rendezvous with Mars.

text.p: Scientists worked frantically on Thursday to prepare for the first landing on Mars in 21 years as the Pathfinder space probe neared its target.
"We are back, and we are back to stay this time," declared Wesley Huntress, the Associate Administrator for Space Science at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
The last spacecraft to land on Mars was the Viking mission in 1976.

Huntress said Pathfinder -- with its "Mars buggy," the Rover -- was the first of 10 spacecraft that would either land on or orbit the planet over the next eight years, culminating in the actual collection of rocks and their return to Earth.

Meanwhile, the 200-strong Pathfinder crew at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena were preparing for any eventuality when the craft touches down at 10:07 a.m. PDT (1707 GMT) on Friday for an Independence Day landing.

"At 4 a.m. Pacific time (11OO GMT), Pathfinder entered Mars' influence. I think it's safe to say we are all under Mars' influence down here as well," Brian Muirhead, the deputy project manager, told reporters.

Muirhead and his colleagues were unable to contain their excitement at the prospect of a hugely successful mission, but were mindful of the possibility that something could go wrong and the mission might end in failure. "We are actually thinking about all the things that could go wrong and how we might respond to them," Mission Manager Richard Cook said.
He said every possible contingency had been considered and possible responses tested.
NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin, visiting JPL for the landing, said failure of the Pathfinder mission would have no impact on the long-term Mars exploration program.
"The success or failure of this first step doesn't relate to the total program," Goldin said, adding that the program was "tolerant" of a few failures.
"I want people to take risks. I want them to know that if they fail, we will come to them and shake their hands" he said.

As he spoke, Pathfinder and its precious cargo were hurtling toward Mars at 12,000 miles per hour (19,300 kph), a speed that was due to increase to 16,000 mph (25,750 kph) as the spacecraft was pulled toward the planet. It is set to slam into the Martian atmosphere at that speed about 10:03 a.m. PDT (1703 GMT) on Friday, four minutes before touchdown.

The spacecraft was 280,000 miles (450,604 km) away from its rendezvous with Mars on Thursday morning. By 7:45 p.m. PDT on Thursday (0245 GMT on Friday) it was due to be the same distance from Mars as the moon is from Earth; about 250,000 miles (402,300 km).
If all goes to plan, Pathfinder will deploy its parachute two minutes before landing and turn on its radar sensors 90 seconds later as it heads for the Martian plane known as Ares Vallis.

When the radar senses the distance from the planet's surface is correct it will deploy a parachute, which will reduce the craft's speed from 1,000 mph (1,609 kph) to 45 to 55 mph (70 to 90 kph) when it makes contact with the surface.

Huge airbags surrounding the lander will be inflated just eight seconds before hitting the Martian surface. Pathfinder will initially bounce along the Martian surface like a beach ball, except that the bounces will start out at 40 feet (12 metres) high and 100 yards (90 metres) long.

But whether the landing has been successful will not be known for a nailbiting four-plus hours from the scheduled touchdown. Scientists explained that during the landing, the Earth will be on the Martian horizon and no communication with the spacecraft will be possible.
